name: Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline

lead: Gly-Pro-Hyp is one of the small peptides produced when collagen is broken down into the hydrolysates sold as oral collagen supplements and used in some cosmetics. People take those supplements for firmer, more hydrated, less wrinkled skin.

The idea is that collagen peptides are absorbed after eating and signal to skin fibroblasts. In rats, hydrolysates are reported to enter the blood partly as intact peptides. Research on this tripeptide covers how it is measured in products and how it is absorbed in laboratory and animal work; human skin trials have used collagen hydrolysates rather than the isolated peptide.

paras: It is taken as part of collagen hydrolysate powders, drinks or capsules as a daily supplement, and it is also found in some cosmetic products.
No safety data specific to the isolated tripeptide were found. It is not a regulated drug.

angle.text: Gly-Pro-Hyp is a collagen-derived tripeptide found in oral collagen supplements, taken for skin firmness and wrinkles. It is absorbed in animals and is thought to signal skin fibroblasts. Human skin trials have used collagen hydrolysates rather than the peptide itself.

lead: Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline (Gly-Pro-Hyp) is a tripeptide made of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, a sequence characteristic of collagen. It is found in collagen hydrolysates, the ingredient in oral collagen supplements and some cosmetic products, and is one of several small peptides studied as a bioactive component of those preparations [1][2].
Available sources describe its measurement and absorption in laboratory and animal work. No study identified here tests the isolated tripeptide for skin appearance in humans.

paras: Collagen hydrolysates contain bioactive dipeptides and tripeptides, among them Gly-Pro-Hyp. A 2024 analytical study developed a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry method to quantify three such peptides, including Gly-Pro-Hyp, in commercial hydrolysates, reflecting their use in health, cosmetic and therapeutic products [2].

In rats given radiolabelled preparations, a low-molecular-weight collagen hydrolysate raised plasma radioactivity quickly and was reported to be absorbed into the blood in peptide form, with the Gly-Pro-Hyp label used as one tracer. That study also examined effects on osteoporosis in the animals [1].

No studies found. Related work consists of animal absorption research [1] and analytical profiling of supplements [2]; clinical research on collagen hydrolysates as a whole exists but was not reviewed here.
